question: What concerns did customers raise about pricing?

resolution.read_instruction: Extract every concern, objection, complaint or question the customer raised about pricing, cost, budget, discounts, contract terms or value for money, quoting the customer's words where possible and noting who raised it and how OrbitFlow responded.
assumptions: No specific company named, so the question covers all calls.
Customers is read broadly to include prospects and existing customers, since prospects also raise pricing concerns.

findings.speaker: Rachel Morgan
findings.quote: It's more than I expected. And I know why — I'd mentally benchmarked this against Zapier, which is not a fair comparison, but that's the number that was in my head.
findings.context: Rachel Morgan found the quoted Growth price higher than expected and had benchmarked OrbitFlow mentally against Zapier; Maya Chen responded that it is a common anchor and the wrong one. — Customer pricing concern raised right after OrbitFlow stated tier pricing; Maya deferred a firm number until the user model is known.

findings.speaker: Rachel Morgan
findings.quote: I can probably still justify it if we replace enough manual work, and maybe some of what we're paying Gainsight for. But I'd need a clearer ROI story than "it saves time."
findings.context: Rachel Morgan said she could justify the cost only with replacing enough manual work and possibly some Gainsight spend, and needs a clearer ROI story than time savings. — Value-for-money concern; she explicitly ties justification to a stronger ROI case.

findings.speaker: Rachel Morgan
findings.quote: I would not sell this internally as headcount reduction. It wouldn't survive contact with my CFO and it's also not true.
findings.context: Rachel Morgan said she would not sell the case internally as headcount reduction; the stronger case is consistency and speed. — Value concern about how the ROI can be presented to finance; OrbitFlow proposed baselining pilot metrics.

findings.speaker: Rachel Morgan
findings.quote: Please make that explicit in the proposal. I do not want to find out in month four that every occasional approver needs a full seat.
findings.context: Rachel Morgan asked that the proposal make the user model explicit, fearing occasional approvers would need full seats later. — Per-seat licensing concern; Maya said pricing would be itemised and gave no exact number.

findings.speaker: Rachel Morgan
findings.quote: A commercial model without hidden scaling surprises.
findings.context: Rachel Morgan wants a commercial model without hidden scaling surprises as a condition for moving to decision. — Pricing condition for decision; Maya said a perfectly valid outcome is not buying if the existing approach is cheaper.

findings.speaker: Tom Alvarez
findings.quote: And there's an engineering cost nobody sees. A script takes two days to write and then quietly eats a few hours every month forever.
findings.context: Tom Alvarez noted that engineering maintenance cost of scripts is an unseen cost not in original estimates. — Total-cost concern; OrbitFlow suggested baselining engineer hours maintaining current process.

findings.speaker: Rachel Morgan
findings.quote: The real commercial question is whether we expand the Workato contract we already have instead of adding another vendor.
findings.context: Rachel Morgan said the real commercial question is whether to expand the existing Workato contract instead of adding another vendor. — Competitive/budget objection; Maya agreed to write it as a pilot exit criterion.

findings.speaker: Rachel Morgan
findings.quote: Finance gets involved above twenty-five thousand a year, so — yes, finance gets involved.
findings.context: Finance involvement is required above twenty-five thousand a year, which affects the cost approval path. — Budget governance detail raised by the customer.

findings.speaker: Priya Shah
findings.quote: What counts as a user? Because we'd have a small number of builders and a lot of people who only approve something or get a notification.
findings.context: Customer asked what counts as a licensed user, since most people only approve or receive notifications rather than build. — Concern about per-seat cost exposure. OrbitFlow said builders and full workspace users are licensed, approval-only or notification-only can be structured differently, and declined to quote a figure until the user model is known.

findings.speaker: Priya Shah
findings.quote: Please make that explicit in the proposal when it comes. I don't want to discover in month four that every occasional approver needs a full seat.
findings.context: Customer does not want occasional approvers to force full seat licences later on. — Forward-looking licensing concern. OrbitFlow committed to an itemised proposal covering builders, viewers, approvers, volume and one-time services separately.

findings.speaker: Priya Shah
findings.quote: It's already covered by our Microsoft agreement, which matters a lot to procurement.
findings.context: Customer's procurement weighs heavily that Power Automate is already covered by an existing Microsoft agreement, so a new spend must justify itself against that. — Cost comparison framing. OrbitFlow agreed a full migration off Microsoft would lose on licensing; customer agreed.

findings.speaker: Priya Shah
findings.quote: A commercial model without hidden scaling surprises.
findings.context: Customer's success criteria for any commercial model require no hidden scaling surprises in cost. — Stated as a condition for moving to a decision; OrbitFlow had given Growth pricing from 1800 a month for up to 30 users and said Enterprise is custom-priced.

findings.speaker: Sophie Reed
findings.quote: Eighteen hundred a month is hard for a team our size. I had something closer to eight hundred, maybe a thousand, in my head.
findings.context: Customer said Growth tier price of 1,800 per month is hard for a team their size; they had expected roughly 800-1,000 per month. OrbitFlow acknowledged the gap. — Price objection raised right after OrbitFlow stated Growth pricing; Leo responded 'That's a real gap. I'm not going to pretend it isn't.'

findings.speaker: Sophie Reed
findings.quote: I could potentially do an annual prepay if that materially changes the number. Does it?
findings.context: Customer asked whether an annual prepay would materially change the price; OrbitFlow said it gives a meaningful discount but not a halving. — Discount probe by customer; vendor limited expectations.

findings.speaker: Sophie Reed
findings.quote: Above that it goes to the COO and the finance director.
findings.context: Customer said the decision is above their own spending authority (15,000 per year), so the 1,800/month (21,600/year) price goes to the COO and finance director, a slower process. — Budget authority constraint raised in response to price; customer noted it is a slower conversation.

findings.speaker: Sophie Reed
findings.quote: budget is the biggest risk here. We could decide we're simply over-buying, and keep Zapier
findings.context: Customer said budget is the biggest risk and they might simply be over-buying, keeping Zapier instead. — Customer stated the value does not yet close the gap versus tools already paid for; OrbitFlow said it would rather they conclude that in July.

findings.speaker: Sophie Reed
findings.quote: I'm just not yet convinced the value closes the gap between this and the tools we already pay for.
findings.context: Customer said they are not yet convinced the value closes the gap between OrbitFlow and tools they already pay for. — Value-for-money concern at end of call; OrbitFlow called it a fair position.

findings.speaker: Sophie Reed
findings.quote: the two hundred doesn't include the four hours a week you spend chasing broken ones.
findings.context: Customer pointed out the current Zapier bill (about 200 per month) excludes staff time spent chasing broken automations (more than four hours a week), so the true current cost is higher; Marcus said he did not know the cost and had never been asked to count it. — Cost-of-status-quo discussion; OrbitFlow suggested four weeks of logging time.

findings.speaker: Sophie Reed
findings.quote: Everyone says that and then there's a surprise later.
findings.context: Customer asked whether per-workflow-run and premium-connector usage adds cost; expressed distrust of later surprise charges. — Usage-based pricing question; OrbitFlow said usage is scoped on runs and premium connectors and would model it.

findings.speaker: Sophie Reed
findings.quote: I can't put "vibes" in a spreadsheet for the finance director.
findings.context: Customer said Zapier's Growth-level pricing gap is tied to the need for a budget case; they cannot put 'vibes' in a spreadsheet for finance. — Customer explained difficulty building the cost business case for the finance director.

findings.speaker: Martin Vogel
findings.quote: The headline licence price is not going to surprise me. We buy enterprise software. What I care about is transparency around professional services, premium connectors, and anything we would only discover after an architecture review. That is where the surprises live.
findings.context: Martin Vogel does not expect the headline licence price to be a surprise, but wants transparency on professional services, premium connectors, and costs that only emerge after architecture review. OrbitFlow (Maya Chen) responded by committing to separate line items with written assumptions and 'to be determined after architecture review' where unknown, rather than placeholder numbers. — Customer raised a concern about hidden costs; vendor response was a commitment to price transparency in the proposal. Vendor (T123) had earlier raised that significant SAP/on-premise work would be professional services and said she'd price it up front.

findings.speaker: Martin Vogel
findings.quote: Thank you. That is exactly the thing I was going to raise later.
findings.context: Martin Vogel welcomed the vendor raising professional services cost early, saying it was what he had planned to raise later. — Customer reaction to vendor volunteering that phase one SAP and on-premise work would be professional services.

findings.speaker: Anika Bose
findings.quote: What is a user? We may have twenty people building and several hundred who only approve something.
findings.context: Anika Bose asked what counts as a licensed user, because DeltaWorks may have about twenty builders and several hundred approval-only users. OrbitFlow (Jon/Maya) declined to give a number until the user model was defined, and said approval-only populations can be structured differently depending on package. — Customer question about per-user licensing model and seat count; vendor would not quote a figure yet.

findings.speaker: Anika Bose
findings.quote: Please put that in the proposal explicitly. I do not want to discover in year two that every occasional approver requires a full seat.
findings.context: Anika Bose required that the proposal explicitly state how occasional approvers are licensed, to avoid paying for a full seat for every approver in year two. OrbitFlow (Maya Chen) agreed it would be explicit. — Customer cost concern about seat licensing for approvers; vendor committed to explicit treatment in proposal.

findings.speaker: Martin Vogel
findings.quote: And there is a maintenance cost that nobody counts — a script takes two days to write and then consumes a few hours every month forever. That never appears in the original estimate.
findings.context: Martin Vogel raised an ongoing maintenance cost of internal scripts that is never counted in original estimates, which he sees as part of the true cost case for automation. He framed it as a value/ROI consideration, not a vendor price objection. — Customer comment on total cost of the status quo and ROI; not a complaint about OrbitFlow pricing.

findings.speaker: Noah Williams
findings.quote: Usage overages. If the bill becomes unpredictable as volumes grow, finance will dislike it even if the base price is fine. I've been through this with two other vendors and both times the second-year invoice was the problem, not the first.
findings.context: Customer worried that usage overages could make the bill unpredictable as volumes grow, and that the second-year invoice would be the real problem. OrbitFlow (Leo) responded by offering to model expected volumes and agree the above-threshold overage mechanism in the contract before signing. — Noah raised it as a finance concern based on two prior vendor experiences; Leo answered that usage is scoped on workflow runs and premium connector needs.

findings.speaker: Noah Williams
findings.quote: Can you cap it?
findings.context: Customer asked whether the usage cost could be capped. OrbitFlow (Leo) declined to promise a specific cap structure before modelling volumes, saying mechanisms exist but a cap might have conditions. — Direct follow-up to the overage concern; Leo deferred a firm answer.

findings.speaker: Noah Williams
findings.quote: Make that split explicit in the proposal. I don't want to find out in year two that every approver needs a full seat.
findings.context: Customer wants the licence split between builders and approval-only or view-only users made explicit in the proposal, to avoid discovering in year two that every approver needs a full seat. — Customer described about 40 builders and up to 300 approve/view users; Leo said approval-only populations can be structured differently and committed to an itemised proposal.

findings.speaker: Hannah Cole
findings.quote: Three hundred is optimistic, by the way. It might be more.
findings.context: Customer said the 300-user count is probably optimistic and could grow, which raises seat cost exposure. OrbitFlow (Leo) agreed to model 300 and 500 users to show the cost curve. — Hannah first said it might be more; Noah corrected to 'It's three hundred today', then Hannah agreed.

findings.speaker: Noah Williams
findings.quote: The range is roughly where I expected an enterprise workflow product to land. That's not my concern.
findings.context: Customer said the Enterprise price range was roughly what they expected for an enterprise workflow product, so base price is not their concern. — Said after Leo gave the Growth price (eighteen hundred a month up to thirty users) and said Enterprise is custom priced.

findings.speaker: Noah Williams
findings.quote: That's cheaper and it's what someone will propose.
findings.context: Customer noted that keeping scripts and documenting them is cheaper and will likely be proposed internally as an alternative to OrbitFlow, which is a value-for-money pressure. — Raised in the competitive discussion; Hannah agreed it would be proposed and would waste about two months. Leo answered by addressing it in pilot criteria.

findings.speaker: Noah Williams
findings.quote: But I'd like the overage modelling done in parallel rather than after, because if the economics don't work at scale I'd rather know in week two than week six.
findings.context: Customer wants overage economics modelled in parallel with the pilot so they know early if pricing fails at scale. — Customer said nothing binding was needed before the pilot, but asked for the commercial modelling early.

findings.speaker: Imogen Price
findings.quote: That's above what I had in mind.
findings.context: Customer found the Growth package price above her budget expectation. — Initial reaction to OrbitFlow's quoted price; OrbitFlow responded that it is good value relative to what is being replaced.

findings.speaker: Imogen Price
findings.quote: Is there any way to start with ten users? Or bill monthly while we prove the process before committing for a year?
findings.context: Customer asked whether Fable could start with ten users and/or pay monthly instead of committing to an annual agreement, to prove the process first. — Customer's request for flexible terms; OrbitFlow said monthly was 'usually fine' but needed manager approval, and later said it would confirm.

findings.speaker: Imogen Price
findings.quote: So I'd be paying for twenty seats I don't need.
findings.context: Customer objected to paying for thirty seats when she needs about ten; OrbitFlow said the thirty-user package is fixed. — Seat-count concern about package pricing; OrbitFlow said 'the price is the price'.

findings.speaker: Imogen Price
findings.quote: It's a hard limit. And more to the point, if I have to take it to him, he'll ask what we get for twenty-one thousand that we don't get from Zapier for two thousand, and I need a better answer than "it's more robust."
findings.context: Ben noted the annual cost is about £21.5k, and Imogen said her spending authority is capped at £20k, with the founder approving anything above that. — Budget authority constraint that makes the price a blocker; OrbitFlow asked if the limit was hard and got a 'hard limit' answer.

findings.speaker: Imogen Price
findings.quote: We're an agency, Alastair. Nobody's auditing our onboarding process.
findings.context: Customer questioned the value of OrbitFlow's governance and audit features versus the price, saying an agency has no audit need. — Value-for-money challenge; OrbitFlow's audit-trail value argument was rejected by the customer.

findings.speaker: Imogen Price
findings.quote: Price and complexity are the two risks. And honestly, we may well decide that Zapier plus better process discipline is good enough
findings.context: Customer said Zapier, at about two thousand, is the cheaper alternative and that they may stick with Zapier plus process discipline, which the customer frames as a price and complexity risk. — Competitive price comparison; OrbitFlow argued they'd be back in eighteen months, and the customer replied they would have saved £21k in the meantime.

findings.speaker: Imogen Price
findings.quote: A reference in an agency would be useful, if you've got one.
findings.context: OrbitFlow's sales rep gave a 'lost client worth it' justification in response to price objections; the customer did not accept it as a value answer, and asked for a reference showing the account's outcome instead. — OrbitFlow's anecdote about a prior deal; the customer and Ben pressed on whether the onboarding problem was actually solved.

findings.speaker: Carlos Mendes
findings.quote: For us to work around all of that, OrbitFlow has to be materially better, not marginally better.
findings.context: Customer says OrbitFlow must be materially better than the embedded Power Automate, since it is already licensed and approved, to justify switching. — Value-for-money concern tied to the incumbent's licensing; OrbitFlow (Maya) responded by asking what 'materially better' would look like, and Lucy and Carlos named troubleshooting and reusability.

findings.speaker: Carlos Mendes
findings.quote: And we get favourable licensing on it, which matters more than I'd like it to.
findings.context: Customer says Power Automate's favourable licensing matters more than they would like it to. — Cost concern about the incumbent's licensing position; Maya did not dispute it.

findings.speaker: Lucy Hart
findings.quote: What about the Power Automate licensing thing? Because that's genuinely part of the comparison.
findings.context: Customer raised Power Automate licensing as part of the comparison and asked how OrbitFlow compares on it. — Question about licence cost versus the incumbent; Maya replied that OrbitFlow cannot beat bundled licensing on price and that the argument must be operational cost.

findings.speaker: Carlos Mendes
findings.quote: The price might be defensible for central operations. What I need to understand is the licensing model.
findings.context: Customer says the price may be defensible for central operations but needs to understand the licensing model. — Pricing response to Maya's commercials (Growth at 1,800 a month up to 30 users; Enterprise custom). Maya did not give a number, citing the need for builder versus approver counts.

findings.speaker: Carlos Mendes
findings.quote: They should not need full seats. If your model says they do, this is over before it starts.
findings.context: Customer warns that per-seat licensing for hundreds of occasional supervisors would end the deal. — Seat-count concern: supervisors approve or view roughly once a week and should not need full seats. Maya said approval-only populations can be structured differently depending on the package, but gave no number.

findings.speaker: Carlos Mendes
findings.quote: Six builders, several hundred approvers.
findings.context: Customer stated the licensed population: six builders and several hundred approvers. — Lucy gave the builder count (her team of four plus two regional specialists). Carlos summarised the approver population. Maya asked for this shape to be explicit in writing before any proposal.

findings.speaker: Carlos Mendes
findings.quote: That's the argument I'd have to make internally, yes.
findings.context: Customer says the case for switching has to rest on operational cost, not licence cost, and that making it internally is the argument they would need to make. — Carlos accepted Maya's framing that six people fielding troubleshooting tickets may outweigh the licence delta. Maya suggested measuring the time, and Carlos agreed to measure it. Lucy's day-a-week figure was a guess, as the call later confirmed.

findings.speaker: Samir Khan
findings.quote: We end up spending a great deal to automate something that saves a business services person four hours a week.
findings.context: Samir Khan questioned whether the integration effort is disproportionate to the value, expecting a great deal of spend to automate something that saves only about four hours a week. — Value-for-money concern about cost versus benefit. OrbitFlow (Leo) responded that the test is an honest services estimate set against the cost of matter-opening delay, and that the delay cost is client-facing and not four hours a week.

findings.speaker: Eleanor Brooks
findings.quote: Do we have a number for what it costs?
findings.context: Eleanor Brooks asked whether there is a cost figure for delayed matter opening and admitted the firm has none, only time-to-open data. — Customer lacks a cost basis to justify spend. Leo responded that the client-facing cost of delay is the real number to use.

findings.speaker: Samir Khan
findings.quote: It's also harder to evidence.
findings.context: Samir Khan said the value of the delay cost is harder to evidence. — Follow-on to the value question; Eleanor responded that everything worth measuring is harder to evidence.

findings.speaker: Eleanor Brooks
findings.quote: The enterprise range itself doesn't worry me. We buy expensive software.
findings.context: Eleanor Brooks said the enterprise price range does not worry her but that scope does, and she would not build a business case around privileged-content use because it would be rejected. — Customer accepts the Enterprise pricing tier but ties any business case to low-risk operational scope. OrbitFlow (Leo) agreed to scope the proposal to the low-risk tier and mark privileged content out of scope rather than as an upsell.

findings.speaker: Samir Khan
findings.quote: What's a user? We'd have very few builders and a very large number of partners who approve something occasionally.
findings.context: Samir Khan asked how users are defined, noting few builders and many occasional partner approvers, which bears on per-seat licensing cost. — Pricing-model question. Leo declined to give a number without the licence split between builders/full users and approval-only or notification-only users.

findings.speaker: Eleanor Brooks
findings.quote: If it turns out every partner needs a seat, this is a very short conversation.
findings.context: Eleanor Brooks said that if every partner needs a seat, the deal would be a very short conversation, and asked for the seat split in writing. — Customer signals that per-seat cost could end the deal. Leo agreed to surface the split before the customer takes anything internally.

findings.speaker: Eleanor Brooks
findings.quote: That's the thing that goes wrong.
findings.context: Eleanor Brooks and Samir Khan reacted positively to OrbitFlow saying professional services would be quoted separately with assumptions, after noting that implementation costs are usually where things go wrong. — Customer concern about hidden implementation costs appearing after discovery. Leo committed to a separate services line with its assumptions shown.

findings.speaker: Olivia Grant
findings.quote: I think the price is reasonable if it lets us consolidate several manual programmes.
findings.context: Olivia Grant says the price is reasonable only if it lets Inkwell consolidate several manual programmes, making value conditional on consolidation. — Conditional value-for-money view; the consolidation list (spreadsheet, review meeting, part of Gainsight spend) is what justifies the price to her.

findings.speaker: Olivia Grant
findings.quote: I know we're not going to switch it off. I'm saying the spend is questionable.
findings.context: Olivia Grant questions the existing Gainsight spend, which she says is questionable and tied to the cost comparison. — Raised in response to the price discussion. Darren Wu agrees the spend is questionable but calls it a separate matter. Maya Chen said a cost model comparing OrbitFlow with expanding Gainsight will surface it.

findings.speaker: Darren Wu
findings.quote: The spend is very questionable. But that's a separate fight.
findings.context: Darren Wu says the Gainsight spend is very questionable but treats it as a separate issue from this purchase. — Darren pushes back on Olivia's framing, though Olivia replies that it is a related fight.

findings.speaker: Darren Wu
findings.quote: Which is why I want the model to be honest. If the answer is "expand Gainsight, it's cheaper", I want to be able to say that.
findings.context: Customers want a cost model that compares OrbitFlow with expanding Gainsight, including implementation effort on both sides, and Darren wants it to be honest even if Gainsight comes out cheaper. — Olivia links the earlier Gainsight failure to implementation effort, not licensing. Maya Chen agreed to build the comparison that way and said she would rather lose than hide a cheaper Gainsight answer.

findings.speaker: Olivia Grant
findings.quote: I don't want to find out in month four that all sixty-two need full seats.
findings.context: Olivia Grant is concerned that seat licensing could be higher than expected, especially for CSMs who only receive tasks. — Seat counts were given as 3-4 builders and 62 CSMs (Darren confirmed 62). Maya Chen said the proposal would itemise the builder/recipient split and assumptions, and she would not quote a figure yet.

findings.speaker: Darren Wu
findings.quote: That's the argument, and it's a good one, but it relies on the counterfactual. We'd need to be able to say the intervention caused the renewal, and we can't.
findings.context: Darren Wu challenges the ROI argument for renewal retention because the renewal impact cannot be attributed to intervention, and says finance is sceptical of customer success business cases. — Olivia's ROI case relies on intervention preventing non-renewals. Maya Chen responded by proposing a leading indicator (time from first signal to first intervention) that is measurable and attributable.

findings.speaker: Olivia Grant
findings.quote: Finance can say not yet, which is the same thing in practice.
findings.context: Olivia Grant says finance can effectively block the purchase by saying 'not yet'. — Finance is one of the approvers, alongside IT security. Timing is tied to the late-September decision date.

findings.speaker: Maya Chen
findings.quote: I won't quote a figure today because without that split any figure I give would mislead you in one direction or the other.
findings.context: Maya Chen (OrbitFlow) gave only the list price for the Growth tier and declined to quote a total until seat assumptions were split out. — OrbitFlow's response to the pricing questions. Growth is listed at 1800 per month up to thirty users on an annual agreement; Enterprise is custom priced.

findings.speaker: Ava Sinclair
findings.quote: What I do not want is to pay you per event.
findings.context: Customer worried OrbitFlow pricing would charge per event, and Ava does not want to pay per event for high-volume Segment traffic; OrbitFlow advised filtering events upstream so only business-relevant events are sent. — Customer concern about event-based cost; vendor response was architectural (filter in AWS) rather than a price change.

findings.speaker: Marcus Chen
findings.quote: my question is whether usage limits make high-volume event processing uneconomic compared with keeping the event-handling layer in AWS.
findings.context: Marcus asked whether usage limits make high-volume event processing uneconomic compared with keeping event handling in AWS. — Customer cost/value question raised after vendor quoted pricing; vendor said partly, depends on what counts as a run.

findings.speaker: Ava Sinclair
findings.quote: if it's six, the composition pattern you're recommending is also the expensive pattern, and that's a conflict I'd want surfaced before we commit.
findings.context: Customer asked whether a workflow fanning out to five subflows counts as one run or six, and said if it is six the recommended composition pattern is also the expensive pattern. — Billing-unit concern; vendor could not state billing semantics from memory and promised a written answer.

findings.speaker: Ava Sinclair
findings.quote: What's the actual pricing unit?
findings.context: Customer asked for the actual pricing unit; vendor answered that usage is scoped on workflow runs and premium connector needs, with Growth at 1800 a month up to thirty users annual, and flagged Enterprise given security requirements. — Direct pricing question; vendor gave the Growth figure and pointed to Enterprise.

findings.speaker: Marcus Chen
findings.quote: The base price seems plausible.
findings.context: Marcus said the base price seems plausible but raised the usage-limit economics as the open question. — Customer reaction to quoted base price; conditional on usage limits.

findings.speaker: Marcus Chen
findings.quote: I'd like the pricing model in writing before the evaluation ends, not after. If the economics don't work I'd rather know in week three.
findings.context: Customer asked for the pricing model in writing before the evaluation ends so economics can be assessed early. — Commercial request; vendor committed to week two.

findings.speaker: Marcus Chen
findings.quote: Building it is a sprint. Owning it is forever.
findings.context: Customer raised the possibility of building internally to avoid vendor cost, and Marcus framed build versus buy as a cost of ownership question. — Build-vs-buy value concern; not a direct price objection.

findings.speaker: Fiona Bright
findings.quote: Were we charged for those?
findings.context: Customer questioned whether overage charges were applied and was told two of the overages were waived; she states the run tier is wrong, pointing to a pricing/tier concern. — Customer concern about overage billing and run tier; OrbitFlow (Maya Chen) responded that two of four overages were waived (March retry storm, May proactive flag).

findings.speaker: Fiona Bright
findings.quote: But it does mean the run tier is wrong.
findings.context: Customer said the run tier is wrong after overages, implying the current contracted volume is mis-sized and costing them. — Follow-on to overage discussion; OrbitFlow agreed the run tier is wrong and moved to propose a higher tier.

findings.speaker: Devan Shah
findings.quote: from our side we did nothing wrong and it cost us twenty thousand runs.
findings.context: Customer said the March retry storm cost them twenty thousand runs they felt were not their fault, questioning whether they are being charged for vendor-side or unavoidable usage. — Customer pushed back on run consumption from an incident; OrbitFlow said configuration could help but downstream outages will still burn runs.

findings.speaker: Fiona Bright
findings.quote: Braced for "here's a fifteen percent uplift, sign here."
findings.context: Customer was braced for a large price increase (fifteen percent) and expressed relief when told the uplift was seven percent. — Customer expectation about renewal uplift; OrbitFlow confirmed a seven percent list uplift applying to all customers.

findings.speaker: Devan Shah
findings.quote: Can you show that? The two things separately?
findings.context: Customer questioned whether the seat reduction and run tier increase are being used to inflate the total; asked for the two changes to be shown separately because a finance director will ask what changed. — Customer scrutiny of renewal pricing structure; OrbitFlow committed to itemised line items and said the seat reduction is genuine.

findings.speaker: Fiona Bright
findings.quote: Nine percent for forty percent more capacity and a new use case.
findings.context: Customer reacted to the total renewal increase, framing nine percent as a price for forty percent more capacity plus a new use case, indicating value-for-money evaluation. — Customer weighing value; OrbitFlow said total is about nine percent above this year, or about fourteen if nine seats kept.

findings.speaker: Fiona Bright
findings.quote: What about multi-year? Is there anything in it for us?
findings.context: Customer asked about multi-year discount and whether there is anything in it for them; wanted the discount quantified before deciding. — Customer asking about term-based savings; OrbitFlow said a two-year term fixes year-two uplift and discount needs modelling.

findings.speaker: Devan Shah
findings.quote: What's the delta between three fifty and four hundred?
findings.context: Customer asked whether the price of the four hundred thousand tier versus three hundred fifty is a meaningful step, seeking the delta between tiers. — Customer cost question on tier options; OrbitFlow said exact numbers would follow and the step is smaller.

findings.speaker: Fiona Bright
findings.quote: Would you do three years?
findings.context: Customer asked whether a three-year term would be right, and was steered to two years by OrbitFlow. — Customer considering term length; OrbitFlow recommended two years rather than three.

findings.speaker: Graham Attwood
findings.quote: And the honest position — that we're paying for Enterprise and getting very little — matches what I'd concluded myself, which is reassuring.
findings.context: Customer says Pinewood is paying for Enterprise while getting very little value from it. — Graham's view, reached independently and said to be matching his own conclusion. Leo had earlier said Enterprise is probably not worth it for what they use. This is value-for-money concern about the tier.

findings.speaker: Graham Attwood
findings.quote: We've got four builder licences. One person uses it.
findings.context: Customer questions the value of the four builder licences, since only one person uses them. — Raised while discussing why the workflows are stalled. Licence utilisation is a cost/value concern. OrbitFlow's response was to offer enablement, not to change licence count.

draft.answer: Across prospects, renewals, churned customers and cold calls, the most common pricing concern was per-seat licensing for occasional approvers [C1]. Other recurring concerns were a Growth price above expectations or budget authority [C2], hidden usage and services costs [C3], value versus incumbent tools [C4], and cost-justification to finance [C5]. Churned and renewal customers raised paid-for-but-unused value and renewal pricing [C6][C7]. Some customers said base price was not the issue [C8].

claims.text: Many prospects feared that occasional approvers or view-only users would need full seats, and several asked for the user split in writing. Acme Logistics (Rachel Morgan), BrightPath Health (Priya Shah), DeltaWorks (Anika Bose), Ember Financial (Noah Williams, who described about 40 builders and up to 300 approvers), Inkwell Learning (Olivia Grant, 62 CSMs) and Harbor Legal (Samir Khan, Eleanor Brooks) all raised it. Greenline's Carlos Mendes said per-seat licensing for hundreds of supervisors would end the deal. OrbitFlow declined to quote a figure until the user model was defined and committed to itemised proposals.

Several prospects found the Growth price (1,800/month for up to 30 users) too high. Cedar & Finch expected roughly 800-1,000/month, and Sophie Reed's spending authority is 15,000/year, so the decision goes to the COO and finance director. Fable Media's Imogen Price found it above her budget and objected to paying for 30 seats when she needs about 10. Her spending cap is a hard £20k against about £21.5k, and OrbitFlow said the package is fixed. Acme's Rachel Morgan found it above expectations after benchmarking against Zapier, and finance gets involved above 25k there. Trafford Dental's Yvonne Deeks said 1,800/month is not in her budget, wanting 200-300/month, and the opportunity ended on price.

Customers worried about hidden or unpredictable costs. Ember Financial's Noah Williams feared usage overages and a second-year invoice shock, and asked whether usage could be capped. Leo would not promise a cap before modelling volumes. Cedar & Finch distrusted later surprise charges. DeltaWorks' Martin Vogel wanted transparency on professional services and premium connectors. Harbor Legal reacted positively to separately quoted services. Juniper Cloud Tools worried about per-event charges and whether a fan-out counts as one run or six, and Marcus Chen asked for the pricing model in writing. Acme and BrightPath wanted no hidden scaling surprises. Halberd's Grace Okonkwo wanted the AI consumption cost stated as a number.

Prospects questioned value against cheaper or already-licensed alternatives. These were Zapier (Cedar & Finch, Fable Media about £2k vs £21k, Oakhill), Power Automate under existing Microsoft licensing (BrightPath, Greenline), an expanded Workato contract (Acme), a Gainsight comparison (Inkwell), and scripts at Ember. At Greenline, Maya said OrbitFlow cannot beat bundled licensing on price, so the argument must be operational cost.

Customers needed an ROI or business case that finance would accept. Acme's Rachel Morgan wanted a clearer ROI story and would not frame it as headcount reduction. Cedar & Finch's Sophie Reed could not put 'vibes' in a spreadsheet. Harbor Legal had no cost figure for delay. Inkwell's Darren Wu doubted the attribution of renewal ROI. Pinewood's Graham Attwood said 'we'll do some training' would not convince his finance director.

Churned customers said they paid for value they did not use. Oakhill's Hazel Wren paid for Growth with 30 users when four logged in and said the roughly £19k a year was not worth it. She said a plan at £500-600/month would have kept them, and that vendor did not flag the under-use. Verity Payments said they paid a premium for business-user autonomy that did not materialise. Kwame Boateng said price was partly, but not primarily, why they chose Workato. He said they might have accepted a higher price that included paid enablement.

Renewal customers raised several pricing concerns. Lumen Retail's Fiona Bright and Devan Shah said the run tier was wrong, disputed 20,000 runs burned in a March retry storm, and asked for seat reduction and tier increase to be shown separately. Fiona was relieved at a 7% uplift versus the 15% she feared, weighed 9% for 40% more capacity, and asked about multi-year discounts. Pinewood's Graham Attwood and Nadia Rahman said they pay for Enterprise and four builder licences while getting little value, and Graham asked about discounting a six-month term, which was not discounted. Halberd's Grace Okonkwo accepted the 7% uplift without pushback.

Several customers said the base price itself was not their concern. These were Ember Financial's Noah Williams, DeltaWorks' Martin Vogel, Harbor Legal's Eleanor Brooks, Juniper's Marcus Chen (usage economics were the open question) and Greenline's Carlos Mendes (price defensible for central operations, licensing model unclear).

Acme and BrightPath wanted no hidden scaling surprises. Halberd's Grace Okonkwo wanted the AI consumption cost stated as a number.

evidence.speaker: Noah Williams
evidence.quote: Usage overages. If the bill becomes unpredictable as volumes grow, finance will dislike it even if the base price is fine. I've been through this with two other vendors and both times the second-year invoice was the problem, not the first.
evidence.context: Customer worried that usage overages could make the bill unpredictable as volumes grow, and that the second-year invoice would be the real problem. OrbitFlow (Leo) responded by offering to model expected volumes and agree the above-threshold overage mechanism in the contract before signing. — Noah raised it as a finance concern based on two prior vendor experiences; Leo answered that usage is scoped on workflow runs and premium connector needs.

evidence.speaker: Noah Williams
evidence.quote: Can you cap it?
evidence.context: Customer asked whether the usage cost could be capped. OrbitFlow (Leo) declined to promise a specific cap structure before modelling volumes, saying mechanisms exist but a cap might have conditions. — Direct follow-up to the overage concern; Leo deferred a firm answer.

evidence.speaker: Noah Williams
evidence.quote: But I'd like the overage modelling done in parallel rather than after, because if the economics don't work at scale I'd rather know in week two than week six.
evidence.context: Customer wants overage economics modelled in parallel with the pilot so they know early if pricing fails at scale. — Customer said nothing binding was needed before the pilot, but asked for the commercial modelling early.

evidence.speaker: Sophie Reed
evidence.quote: Everyone says that and then there's a surprise later.
evidence.context: Customer asked whether per-workflow-run and premium-connector usage adds cost; expressed distrust of later surprise charges. — Usage-based pricing question; OrbitFlow said usage is scoped on runs and premium connectors and would model it.

evidence.speaker: Martin Vogel
evidence.quote: The headline licence price is not going to surprise me. We buy enterprise software. What I care about is transparency around professional services, premium connectors, and anything we would only discover after an architecture review. That is where the surprises live.
evidence.context: Martin Vogel does not expect the headline licence price to be a surprise, but wants transparency on professional services, premium connectors, and costs that only emerge after architecture review. OrbitFlow (Maya Chen) responded by committing to separate line items with written assumptions and 'to be determined after architecture review' where unknown, rather than placeholder numbers. — Customer raised a concern about hidden costs; vendor response was a commitment to price transparency in the proposal. Vendor (T123) had earlier raised that significant SAP/on-premise work would be professional services and said she'd price it up front.

evidence.speaker: Eleanor Brooks
evidence.quote: That's the thing that goes wrong.
evidence.context: Eleanor Brooks and Samir Khan reacted positively to OrbitFlow saying professional services would be quoted separately with assumptions, after noting that implementation costs are usually where things go wrong. — Customer concern about hidden implementation costs appearing after discovery. Leo committed to a separate services line with its assumptions shown.

evidence.speaker: Ava Sinclair
evidence.quote: What I do not want is to pay you per event.
evidence.context: Customer worried OrbitFlow pricing would charge per event, and Ava does not want to pay per event for high-volume Segment traffic; OrbitFlow advised filtering events upstream so only business-relevant events are sent. — Customer concern about event-based cost; vendor response was architectural (filter in AWS) rather than a price change.

evidence.speaker: Marcus Chen
evidence.quote: my question is whether usage limits make high-volume event processing uneconomic compared with keeping the event-handling layer in AWS.
evidence.context: Marcus asked whether usage limits make high-volume event processing uneconomic compared with keeping event handling in AWS. — Customer cost/value question raised after vendor quoted pricing; vendor said partly, depends on what counts as a run.

evidence.speaker: Ava Sinclair
evidence.quote: if it's six, the composition pattern you're recommending is also the expensive pattern, and that's a conflict I'd want surfaced before we commit.
evidence.context: Customer asked whether a workflow fanning out to five subflows counts as one run or six, and said if it is six the recommended composition pattern is also the expensive pattern. — Billing-unit concern; vendor could not state billing semantics from memory and promised a written answer.

evidence.speaker: Marcus Chen
evidence.quote: I'd like the pricing model in writing before the evaluation ends, not after. If the economics don't work I'd rather know in week three.
evidence.context: Customer asked for the pricing model in writing before the evaluation ends so economics can be assessed early. — Commercial request; vendor committed to week two.

evidence.speaker: Rachel Morgan
evidence.quote: A commercial model without hidden scaling surprises.
evidence.context: Rachel Morgan wants a commercial model without hidden scaling surprises as a condition for moving to decision. — Pricing condition for decision; Maya said a perfectly valid outcome is not buying if the existing approach is cheaper.

evidence.speaker: Priya Shah
evidence.quote: A commercial model without hidden scaling surprises.
evidence.context: Customer's success criteria for any commercial model require no hidden scaling surprises in cost. — Stated as a condition for moving to a decision; OrbitFlow had given Growth pricing from 1800 a month for up to 30 users and said Enterprise is custom-priced.

evidence.speaker: Tobias Lund
evidence.quote: How much?
evidence.context: Customer asked how much the AI usage consumption element will cost. — Raised after the vendor said AI usage has a consumption element beyond the run allocation. Vendor (T097) replied that for about 400 incidents a month it is not material and promised a number in the renewal papers.

evidence.speaker: Grace Okonkwo
evidence.quote: Put the number in anyway.
evidence.context: Customer wanted the AI consumption cost figure stated explicitly, not just described as immaterial. — Follow-up to the consumption cost question. Customer wants a concrete number despite the vendor calling it not material.

claims.text: Prospects questioned value against cheaper or already-licensed alternatives. These were Zapier (Cedar & Finch, Fable Media about £2k vs £21k, Oakhill), Power Automate under existing Microsoft licensing (BrightPath, Greenline), an expanded Workato contract (Acme), a Gainsight comparison (Inkwell), and scripts at Ember. At Greenline, Maya said OrbitFlow cannot beat bundled licensing on price, so the argument must be operational cost.

evidence.speaker: Sophie Reed
evidence.quote: budget is the biggest risk here. We could decide we're simply over-buying, and keep Zapier
evidence.context: Customer said budget is the biggest risk and they might simply be over-buying, keeping Zapier instead. — Customer stated the value does not yet close the gap versus tools already paid for; OrbitFlow said it would rather they conclude that in July.

evidence.speaker: Sophie Reed
evidence.quote: I'm just not yet convinced the value closes the gap between this and the tools we already pay for.
evidence.context: Customer said they are not yet convinced the value closes the gap between OrbitFlow and tools they already pay for. — Value-for-money concern at end of call; OrbitFlow called it a fair position.

evidence.speaker: Imogen Price
evidence.quote: Price and complexity are the two risks. And honestly, we may well decide that Zapier plus better process discipline is good enough
evidence.context: Customer said Zapier, at about two thousand, is the cheaper alternative and that they may stick with Zapier plus process discipline, which the customer frames as a price and complexity risk. — Competitive price comparison; OrbitFlow argued they'd be back in eighteen months, and the customer replied they would have saved £21k in the meantime.

evidence.speaker: Hazel Wren
evidence.quote: About two thousand a year. Maybe two and a half with the tier we need.
evidence.context: Customer says Zapier at about £2,000-£2,500 a year is roughly a tenth of the OrbitFlow cost, and an alternative that makes the OrbitFlow price hard to defend. — Price comparison against a competitor; customer accepts Zapier loses approval steps and run history.

evidence.speaker: Priya Shah
evidence.quote: It's already covered by our Microsoft agreement, which matters a lot to procurement.
evidence.context: Customer's procurement weighs heavily that Power Automate is already covered by an existing Microsoft agreement, so a new spend must justify itself against that. — Cost comparison framing. OrbitFlow agreed a full migration off Microsoft would lose on licensing; customer agreed.

evidence.speaker: Carlos Mendes
evidence.quote: For us to work around all of that, OrbitFlow has to be materially better, not marginally better.
evidence.context: Customer says OrbitFlow must be materially better than the embedded Power Automate, since it is already licensed and approved, to justify switching. — Value-for-money concern tied to the incumbent's licensing; OrbitFlow (Maya) responded by asking what 'materially better' would look like, and Lucy and Carlos named troubleshooting and reusability.

evidence.speaker: Carlos Mendes
evidence.quote: And we get favourable licensing on it, which matters more than I'd like it to.
evidence.context: Customer says Power Automate's favourable licensing matters more than they would like it to. — Cost concern about the incumbent's licensing position; Maya did not dispute it.

evidence.speaker: Lucy Hart
evidence.quote: What about the Power Automate licensing thing? Because that's genuinely part of the comparison.
evidence.context: Customer raised Power Automate licensing as part of the comparison and asked how OrbitFlow compares on it. — Question about licence cost versus the incumbent; Maya replied that OrbitFlow cannot beat bundled licensing on price and that the argument must be operational cost.

evidence.speaker: Rachel Morgan
evidence.quote: The real commercial question is whether we expand the Workato contract we already have instead of adding another vendor.
evidence.context: Rachel Morgan said the real commercial question is whether to expand the existing Workato contract instead of adding another vendor. — Competitive/budget objection; Maya agreed to write it as a pilot exit criterion.

evidence.speaker: Darren Wu
evidence.quote: Which is why I want the model to be honest. If the answer is "expand Gainsight, it's cheaper", I want to be able to say that.
evidence.context: Customers want a cost model that compares OrbitFlow with expanding Gainsight, including implementation effort on both sides, and Darren wants it to be honest even if Gainsight comes out cheaper. — Olivia links the earlier Gainsight failure to implementation effort, not licensing. Maya Chen agreed to build the comparison that way and said she would rather lose than hide a cheaper Gainsight answer.

evidence.speaker: Noah Williams
evidence.quote: That's cheaper and it's what someone will propose.
evidence.context: Customer noted that keeping scripts and documenting them is cheaper and will likely be proposed internally as an alternative to OrbitFlow, which is a value-for-money pressure. — Raised in the competitive discussion; Hannah agreed it would be proposed and would waste about two months. Leo answered by addressing it in pilot criteria.

evidence.speaker: Carlos Mendes
evidence.quote: That's the argument I'd have to make internally, yes.
evidence.context: Customer says the case for switching has to rest on operational cost, not licence cost, and that making it internally is the argument they would need to make. — Carlos accepted Maya's framing that six people fielding troubleshooting tickets may outweigh the licence delta. Maya suggested measuring the time, and Carlos agreed to measure it. Lucy's day-a-week figure was a guess, as the call later confirmed.

claims.text: Customers needed an ROI or business case that finance would accept. Acme's Rachel Morgan wanted a clearer ROI story and would not frame it as headcount reduction. Cedar & Finch's Sophie Reed could not put 'vibes' in a spreadsheet. Harbor Legal had no cost figure for delay. Inkwell's Darren Wu doubted the attribution of renewal ROI. Pinewood's Graham Attwood said 'we'll do some training' would not convince his finance director.

evidence.speaker: Rachel Morgan
evidence.quote: I can probably still justify it if we replace enough manual work, and maybe some of what we're paying Gainsight for. But I'd need a clearer ROI story than "it saves time."
evidence.context: Rachel Morgan said she could justify the cost only with replacing enough manual work and possibly some Gainsight spend, and needs a clearer ROI story than time savings. — Value-for-money concern; she explicitly ties justification to a stronger ROI case.

evidence.speaker: Rachel Morgan
evidence.quote: I would not sell this internally as headcount reduction. It wouldn't survive contact with my CFO and it's also not true.
evidence.context: Rachel Morgan said she would not sell the case internally as headcount reduction; the stronger case is consistency and speed. — Value concern about how the ROI can be presented to finance; OrbitFlow proposed baselining pilot metrics.

evidence.speaker: Sophie Reed
evidence.quote: I can't put "vibes" in a spreadsheet for the finance director.
evidence.context: Customer said Zapier's Growth-level pricing gap is tied to the need for a budget case; they cannot put 'vibes' in a spreadsheet for finance. — Customer explained difficulty building the cost business case for the finance director.

evidence.speaker: Eleanor Brooks
evidence.quote: Do we have a number for what it costs?
evidence.context: Eleanor Brooks asked whether there is a cost figure for delayed matter opening and admitted the firm has none, only time-to-open data. — Customer lacks a cost basis to justify spend. Leo responded that the client-facing cost of delay is the real number to use.

evidence.speaker: Samir Khan
evidence.quote: It's also harder to evidence.
evidence.context: Samir Khan said the value of the delay cost is harder to evidence. — Follow-on to the value question; Eleanor responded that everything worth measuring is harder to evidence.

evidence.speaker: Darren Wu
evidence.quote: That's the argument, and it's a good one, but it relies on the counterfactual. We'd need to be able to say the intervention caused the renewal, and we can't.
evidence.context: Darren Wu challenges the ROI argument for renewal retention because the renewal impact cannot be attributed to intervention, and says finance is sceptical of customer success business cases. — Olivia's ROI case relies on intervention preventing non-renewals. Maya Chen responded by proposing a leading indicator (time from first signal to first intervention) that is measurable and attributable.

evidence.speaker: Graham Attwood
evidence.quote: 'we'll do some training' is not going to convince my finance director.
evidence.context: Customer says the enablement offer must be justified in financial terms because the finance director will need convincing. — Budget concern about the value of the enablement proposal. Ruth and Leo then made enablement free of charge, which answered the concern.

claims.text: Churned customers said they paid for value they did not use. Oakhill's Hazel Wren paid for Growth with 30 users when four logged in and said the roughly £19k a year was not worth it. She said a plan at £500-600/month would have kept them, and that vendor did not flag the under-use. Verity Payments said they paid a premium for business-user autonomy that did not materialise. Kwame Boateng said price was partly, but not primarily, why they chose Workato. He said they might have accepted a higher price that included paid enablement.

evidence.speaker: Hazel Wren
evidence.quote: We were on Growth, at eighteen hundred a month, for thirty users, when we had four people who ever logged in.
evidence.context: Customer says Growth plan at £1,800/month for 30 users was paid for while only four people logged in, so they bought more than they needed. — Core pricing concern: paying for unused seats/capacity on Growth tier; customer frames it as the reason for churn.

evidence.speaker: Hazel Wren
evidence.quote: They're not worth nineteen thousand pounds a year to a company our size.
evidence.context: Customer says the annual cost (about £19k) is hard to justify for a company their size, and that the value of the features they'd lose is not worth that price. — Value-for-money objection; customer says the three things they'd lose matter but are not worth £19k a year to a company their size.

evidence.speaker: Hazel Wren
evidence.quote: If you'd had something at five or six hundred a month I'd still be a customer
evidence.context: Customer says they would have been more likely to keep buying if a smaller, cheaper plan (about £500-£600/month) existed; the entry point of Growth priced them out. — Customer's complaint about the lack of a lower-priced tier; vendor confirmed no such plan exists.

evidence.speaker: Hazel Wren
evidence.quote: Someone should have noticed after six months that we had four users on a thirty-user plan and said something.
evidence.context: Vendor (Ruth) says the account was not monitored for seat under-use, and customer says someone should have flagged the four users on a thirty-user plan. — Customer criticism that vendor did not raise the over-licensing; vendor acknowledged the data is looked at but rarely acted on for accounts this size.

evidence.speaker: Sarah Lindqvist
evidence.quote: the licence cost was being justified by a benefit — business-user autonomy — that wasn't materialising.
evidence.context: Customer said the licence cost was being justified by a business-user autonomy benefit that was not materialising, which was a reason engineering supported leaving. — Value-for-money concern raised by the engineering manager; the stated reason for leaving was value, not only connector gap.

evidence.speaker: Kwame Boateng
evidence.quote: So we paid a premium for a business-user platform and used it as an engineering tool. And as an engineering tool it's fine but it's not worth the premium.
evidence.context: Customer said they paid a premium for a business-user platform but used it as an engineering tool, which was not worth the premium. — Value-for-money objection about the premium paid versus actual use.

evidence.speaker: Kwame Boateng
evidence.quote: Less. Not dramatically less.
evidence.context: Customer said Workato's price is less than OrbitFlow's but not dramatically less, and that price was only partly the reason for switching. — When asked if the switch was a price decision, customer said it was partly price at the margin but not primarily price. OrbitFlow (Maya) asserted it was not a price decision and customer partially agreed.

evidence.speaker: Kwame Boateng
evidence.quote: It's partly a price decision, because at the margin we could justify one and not the other. But no, it's not primarily price.
evidence.context: Customer said the decision was partly a price decision because at the margin they could justify one platform and not the other. — Qualification of the price factor; customer said it was not primarily price.

evidence.speaker: Kwame Boateng
evidence.quote: 'this is eighty thousand for the platform and twenty-five for six months of someone sitting with your team', I might have said no.
evidence.context: Customer said that for a future purchase they would accept a higher platform cost if paired with a cost for a person to build workflows, suggesting pricing should include the enablement cost. — Customer's pricing suggestion for winning them back; OrbitFlow (Maya) framed it as a product and pricing point.

claims.text: Renewal customers raised several pricing concerns. Lumen Retail's Fiona Bright and Devan Shah said the run tier was wrong, disputed 20,000 runs burned in a March retry storm, and asked for seat reduction and tier increase to be shown separately. Fiona was relieved at a 7% uplift versus the 15% she feared, weighed 9% for 40% more capacity, and asked about multi-year discounts. Pinewood's Graham Attwood and Nadia Rahman said they pay for Enterprise and four builder licences while getting little value, and Graham asked about discounting a six-month term, which was not discounted. Halberd's Grace Okonkwo accepted the 7% uplift without pushback.

evidence.speaker: Fiona Bright
evidence.quote: Were we charged for those?
evidence.context: Customer questioned whether overage charges were applied and was told two of the overages were waived; she states the run tier is wrong, pointing to a pricing/tier concern. — Customer concern about overage billing and run tier; OrbitFlow (Maya Chen) responded that two of four overages were waived (March retry storm, May proactive flag).

evidence.speaker: Fiona Bright
evidence.quote: But it does mean the run tier is wrong.
evidence.context: Customer said the run tier is wrong after overages, implying the current contracted volume is mis-sized and costing them. — Follow-on to overage discussion; OrbitFlow agreed the run tier is wrong and moved to propose a higher tier.

evidence.speaker: Devan Shah
evidence.quote: from our side we did nothing wrong and it cost us twenty thousand runs.
evidence.context: Customer said the March retry storm cost them twenty thousand runs they felt were not their fault, questioning whether they are being charged for vendor-side or unavoidable usage. — Customer pushed back on run consumption from an incident; OrbitFlow said configuration could help but downstream outages will still burn runs.

evidence.speaker: Devan Shah
evidence.quote: Can you show that? The two things separately?
evidence.context: Customer questioned whether the seat reduction and run tier increase are being used to inflate the total; asked for the two changes to be shown separately because a finance director will ask what changed. — Customer scrutiny of renewal pricing structure; OrbitFlow committed to itemised line items and said the seat reduction is genuine.

evidence.speaker: Fiona Bright
evidence.quote: Braced for "here's a fifteen percent uplift, sign here."
evidence.context: Customer was braced for a large price increase (fifteen percent) and expressed relief when told the uplift was seven percent. — Customer expectation about renewal uplift; OrbitFlow confirmed a seven percent list uplift applying to all customers.

evidence.speaker: Fiona Bright
evidence.quote: Nine percent for forty percent more capacity and a new use case.
evidence.context: Customer reacted to the total renewal increase, framing nine percent as a price for forty percent more capacity plus a new use case, indicating value-for-money evaluation. — Customer weighing value; OrbitFlow said total is about nine percent above this year, or about fourteen if nine seats kept.

evidence.speaker: Fiona Bright
evidence.quote: What about multi-year? Is there anything in it for us?
evidence.context: Customer asked about multi-year discount and whether there is anything in it for them; wanted the discount quantified before deciding. — Customer asking about term-based savings; OrbitFlow said a two-year term fixes year-two uplift and discount needs modelling.

evidence.speaker: Graham Attwood
evidence.quote: And the honest position — that we're paying for Enterprise and getting very little — matches what I'd concluded myself, which is reassuring.
evidence.context: Customer says Pinewood is paying for Enterprise while getting very little value from it. — Graham's view, reached independently and said to be matching his own conclusion. Leo had earlier said Enterprise is probably not worth it for what they use. This is value-for-money concern about the tier.

evidence.speaker: Graham Attwood
evidence.quote: We've got four builder licences. One person uses it.
evidence.context: Customer questions the value of the four builder licences, since only one person uses them. — Raised while discussing why the workflows are stalled. Licence utilisation is a cost/value concern. OrbitFlow's response was to offer enablement, not to change licence count.

evidence.speaker: Nadia Rahman
evidence.quote: Audit export — no. Residency — we're UK only and we're on the EU region, so, technically yes, but it's not a requirement anyone's written down.
evidence.context: Customer says they pay for Enterprise features they don't use, such as audit export and a requirement for EU residency that was never documented. — Nadia was asked which Enterprise features they use. OrbitFlow (Leo) then offered a cheaper Growth tier, which was ruled out because it removes SSO.

evidence.speaker: Graham Attwood
evidence.quote: Would you discount six months?
evidence.context: Customer asks whether OrbitFlow would discount a six-month term. — Raised as a question about the shorter renewal option. Leo answered that six months is priced pro-rata at the annual rate with no short-term premium or uplift, and no discount.

evidence.speaker: Grace Okonkwo
evidence.quote: Seven percent on a number that size is not worth an hour of my life.
evidence.context: Customer accepted a seven percent standard uplift on renewal without pushing back, judging it not worth the effort to contest. — Customer raised no objection to the price increase. Vendor (T006) presented it as the only change at renewal; the customer dismissed negotiating over it.

claims.text: Several customers said the base price itself was not their concern. These were Ember Financial's Noah Williams, DeltaWorks' Martin Vogel, Harbor Legal's Eleanor Brooks, Juniper's Marcus Chen (usage economics were the open question) and Greenline's Carlos Mendes (price defensible for central operations, licensing model unclear).

evidence.speaker: Noah Williams
evidence.quote: The range is roughly where I expected an enterprise workflow product to land. That's not my concern.
evidence.context: Customer said the Enterprise price range was roughly what they expected for an enterprise workflow product, so base price is not their concern. — Said after Leo gave the Growth price (eighteen hundred a month up to thirty users) and said Enterprise is custom priced.

evidence.speaker: Martin Vogel
evidence.quote: The headline licence price is not going to surprise me. We buy enterprise software. What I care about is transparency around professional services, premium connectors, and anything we would only discover after an architecture review. That is where the surprises live.
evidence.context: Martin Vogel does not expect the headline licence price to be a surprise, but wants transparency on professional services, premium connectors, and costs that only emerge after architecture review. OrbitFlow (Maya Chen) responded by committing to separate line items with written assumptions and 'to be determined after architecture review' where unknown, rather than placeholder numbers. — Customer raised a concern about hidden costs; vendor response was a commitment to price transparency in the proposal. Vendor (T123) had earlier raised that significant SAP/on-premise work would be professional services and said she'd price it up front.

evidence.speaker: Eleanor Brooks
evidence.quote: The enterprise range itself doesn't worry me. We buy expensive software.
evidence.context: Eleanor Brooks said the enterprise price range does not worry her but that scope does, and she would not build a business case around privileged-content use because it would be rejected. — Customer accepts the Enterprise pricing tier but ties any business case to low-risk operational scope. OrbitFlow (Leo) agreed to scope the proposal to the low-risk tier and mark privileged content out of scope rather than as an upsell.

evidence.speaker: Marcus Chen
evidence.quote: The base price seems plausible.
evidence.context: Marcus said the base price seems plausible but raised the usage-limit economics as the open question. — Customer reaction to quoted base price; conditional on usage limits.

evidence.speaker: Carlos Mendes
evidence.quote: The price might be defensible for central operations. What I need to understand is the licensing model.
evidence.context: Customer says the price may be defensible for central operations but needs to understand the licensing model. — Pricing response to Maya's commercials (Growth at 1,800 a month up to 30 users; Enterprise custom). Maya did not give a number, citing the need for builder versus approver counts.
